source: Wisconsin Administrative Code chapter NR 40 (Invasive Species Identification, Classification and Control), Register November 2024 No. 827

plants.lookFor: A shrub or small tree whose leaves stay green late into fall. Clusters of black, pea-sized berries. Scratch the bark: it's orange inside.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Sigitas Juzėnas, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: Leafs out earlier than native species and produces toxic berries that alter soil chemistry, stopping native regeneration.

plants.lookFor: A shrub with shiny, smooth-edged leaves that stay green into fall, and pea-sized berries that turn from red to dark purple.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: David Perez, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: It forms thick thickets in wetlands and woods that crowd out native plants.
It shades out prairie plants and adds extra nitrogen to the soil, which helps weeds. One plant can make more than 100,000 seeds.
plants.lookFor: A bushy plant 3 to 6 feet tall with leaves in threes (finely toothed) and long spikes of tiny white or yellow flowers that smell very sweet.
A biennial herb whose leaves stay green into winter. Clusters of white, four-petaled flowers. Crush the leaves: they smell like garlic.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Robert Flogaus-Faust, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: Releases underground chemicals (allelopathy) that destroy beneficial soil fungi, effectively poisoning the roots of surrounding native plants.
It looks like a pretty wildflower, but it spreads into woods and crowds out native flowers.
plants.lookFor: Tall stems with loose clusters of 4-petaled flowers (purple, pink or white) that smell sweet at night, and toothed, pointed leaves. Native phlox looks similar but has 5 petals.
A very tall grass with blue-green leaves and big, fluffy plumes like feather dusters, tan to purple.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Eppu, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: The non-native kind grows in tall, thick walls that take over wetlands, but a native kind looks similar, so experts need to check.
It forms huge patches of only itself in wetlands and covers the ground with dead grass, so native plants and insects can't live there.
plants.lookFor: A tall grass (2 to 6 feet) in wet places, with flat leaves and thick seed heads that start green or purple and turn tan. The striped garden kind, ribbon grass, is regulated; this plain green kind isn't.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Robert Flogaus-Faust, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

plants.lookFor: Tall, bamboo-like stems with big spade-shaped leaves, and plumes of tiny cream flowers in late summer.
plants.why: It grows so strong it can push up through pavement, and its thick patches crowd out plants along rivers.
It sends up new sprouts from its roots and grows into thick groves that shade out prairie and savanna plants.
plants.lookFor: A tree with leaves made of 7 to 21 small oval leaflets, droopy clusters of sweet-smelling white flowers in spring, and flat brown seed pods.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Radio Tonreg from Vienna, Austria, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

plants.lookFor: Flat-topped clusters of tiny yellow flowers on tall stems, with leaves split into toothed leaflets. Grows along roadsides and in fields.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Силаева Татьяна Борисовна, CC0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: It takes over roadsides and prairies, and its sap can burn skin when the sun hits it.
plants.warning: Don't touch! The sap can cause painful burns and blisters in sunlight.

plants.lookFor: Tall spikes of pink-purple flowers from late June to September, with stiff, square stems and leaves in pairs.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: George Chernilevsky, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: One plant can make millions of seeds, and it chokes the wetlands that ducks, frogs, and turtles need.
Its big flat leaves smother the plants underneath, and it spreads from roadsides into prairies.
plants.lookFor: A tall, prickly plant with egg-shaped, spiny flower heads that bloom purple from June to October. Its leaves join into a cup around the stem.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: George Chernilevsky, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

plants.why: One plant can drop more than 100,000 seeds, and it crowds out native plants in sunny fields and along roadsides.
plants.lookFor: First year: a flat circle of big, soft, fuzzy gray-green leaves. Second year: one tall stalk (up to 6 feet) covered in small yellow flowers.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: gailhampshire from Cradley, Malvern, U.K, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

plants.why: It takes over sunny, dry places like prairies and makes it hard for other plants to grow nearby.
Birds spread its berries everywhere, and it changes the soil in ways that help it crowd out prairie plants.
Its roots creep underground and pop up as big prickly patches that crowd out other plants.
It forms thorny thickets that deer won't eat, and those thickets can be good homes for ticks.
This vine smothers other plants and tricks monarch butterflies into laying eggs where caterpillars can't survive.
Every part of this plant is very poisonous to people and animals.
plants.warning: Don't touch it and never eat it! Every part is very poisonous.

plants.why: This vine grows super fast and can cover and smother whole trees.
This prickly vine grows very fast and smothers other plants under a blanket of leaves.
This vine climbs over shrubs and small trees and blocks their sunlight.
It grows taller than a basketball hoop in thick patches that crowd out plants along rivers.
It carpets the forest floor in spring and crowds out native spring wildflowers.
This bush honeysuckle leafs out early in spring and shades out the wildflowers below it.
This bush honeysuckle forms dense shrubs that crowd out native plants in woods and fields.
This bush honeysuckle spreads when birds eat its berries, and it shades out plants on the forest floor.
This tall bush honeysuckle grows into thick walls of shrubs that block sunlight from everything underneath.
Its very deep roots make it almost impossible to pull out, and its milky sap can irritate skin.
This vine wraps tightly around trees and can strangle them or pull them down.
It grows very fast, sends up new sprouts from its roots, and is a favorite food of the spotted lanternfly pest.
It grows into huge thorny thickets that people and animals can't get through.
This giant plant crowds out others, and its sap can cause bad burns on skin in sunlight.
plants.warning: Don't touch! The sap can cause serious burns and blisters in sunlight.

plants.why: Each big nodding flower can make up to 1,200 seeds, and the prickly plants take over pastures and prairies.
One plant can make up to 10,000 seeds that last more than ten years in the soil.
It makes thick, prickly patches in wet meadows and forest openings.
It grows into thick walls in wetlands and crowds out the plants that ducks, frogs and fish need.
It grows into thick walls in wetlands and crowds out the plants that ducks, frogs and fish need.
A very tall cattail (up to 13 feet) that can take over wetlands. It's prohibited, so report it right away.
A small cattail that is prohibited in Wisconsin, so finding it early really matters.
Its big leaves smother the plants underneath, and it spreads from roadsides into prairies.

groups.lookFor: Bushy shrubs with leaves in pairs, sweet-smelling white, pink or yellow flowers in spring, and red or orange berries. Older branches are hollow inside.
groups.why: They leaf out early in spring and grow into thick bushes that shade out wildflowers and young trees.
groups.photoCredit: Photo: Alex Abair, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

groups.lookFor: Prickly plants with spiny-edged leaves and purple or pink flower heads. Wisconsin also has native thistles, so compare with the DNR pages below.
groups.why: They spread lots of wind-blown seeds (Canada thistle also spreads by creeping roots) and their prickly patches crowd out native plants.
groups.photoCredit: Photo: Robert Flogaus-Faust, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

groups.lookFor: Tall wetland plants with long, flat leaves and a brown, sausage-shaped spike. On the invasive kinds there's a gap between the brown spike and the thin yellow spike above it. The native broad-leaved cattail has no gap.
groups.why: They grow into thick walls that take over wetlands and crowd out the plants that ducks, frogs and fish need.
groups.photoCredit: Photo: Bobby McCabe, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

otherSources: Sweet clover, reed canary grass and common mullein are not in NR 40. Their facts come from the Minnesota DNR (sweet clover, reed canary grass) and Invasive.org (common mullein).
